title: Associations of Admission Phase Angle and Surgical Indication with Functional Status After Hip Surgery: A Retrospective Study.
abstract: Background and Objectives: Phase angle measured by bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) may reflect physiological status following hip surgery. This study compared functional status between patients undergoing surgery for fracture and osteoarthritis (OA) and examined factors associated with low functional status four weeks after rehabilitation admission. Materials and Methods: This retrospective study included 147 patients admitted to a rehabilitation hospital after hip surgery between June 2022 and March 2025, comprising 114 fracture and 33 OA patients. Functional status was assessed using the Berg Balance Scale (BBS), Functional Ambulation Category (FAC), and Korean version of the Modified Barthel Index (K-MBI). Logistic regression models included surgical indication, age, the interval from acute-care discharge to rehabilitation admission, sarcopenia, body mass index, and admission phase angle. Results: The fracture group was older and had lower phase angle and functional scores than the OA group. Adjusted ORs for low functional status in fracture versus OA patients were 6.498 (95% CI, 1.934-21.828) for BBS, 7.360 (2.302-23.536) for FAC, and 3.759 (1.179-11.983) for K-MBI. Corresponding adjusted ORs per 1° higher admission phase angle were 0.521 (95% CI, 0.296-0.918), 0.491 (0.273-0.883), and 0.418 (0.240-0.729), respectively. Conclusions: Surgical indication and admission phase angle were associated with functional status four weeks after rehabilitation admission. These observational associations require cautious interpretation because admission functional scores were not included in the models. The clinical prognostic value of phase angle beyond baseline functional assessment requires further evaluation.

title: Effects of neuromuscular electrical stimulation applied simultaneously with exercise therapy in patellofemoral pain: A single-blind, randomized, sham-controlled pilot trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Simultaneous neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) during exercise may augment task-specific quadriceps activation, but its additional effects in patellofemoral pain (PFP) are uncertain. This pilot trial examined whether adding simultaneous NMES improved pain, knee-related function, dynamic stability, quadriceps strength, and muscle thickness compared with exercise therapy plus sham stimulation.
METHODS: In this single-blind, randomized, sham-controlled pilot trial, 30 participants were allocated 1:1 to an intervention group or acontrol group. Both groups received the same hip- and knee-targeted exercise therapy twice weekly for 6 weeks. The intervention group received NMES during leg press and leg extension exercises, whereas the control group wore the same device with stimulation intensity set to zero. The primary outcome was worst pain during the previous week, assessed using the visual analogue scale(VAS). Secondary outcomes included the anterior knee pain scale (AKPS), Y-Balance Test (YBT) composite score, isokinetic quadriceps strength (60°/s, 180°/s), and quadriceps muscle thickness.
RESULTS: No additional between-group benefit was detected for worst pain (p = .96; Cohen's d = -0.03), AKPS (p = .26; Cohen's d = -0.24), YBT composite (p = .28; Cohen's d = -0.26), isokinetic strength at 60°/s (p = .67; Cohen's d = -0.11), or 180°/s (p = .56; Cohen's d = -0.12). Total quadriceps muscle thickness increased more in the intervention group than in the control group, but the effect was small (p = .03; Cohen's d = -0.27). No adverse events were reported.
CONCLUSION: No additional short-term benefit of adding simultaneous NMES to exercise therapy was detected for pain, knee-related function, dynamic stability, or quadriceps strength compared with exercise therapy plus sham stimulation. A small increase in total quadriceps muscle thickness was detected, but its clinical relevance remains uncertain. These findings do not support routine addition of simultaneous NMES for short-term pain relief or functional improvement.

title: Menstrual Cycle Disorders in Female Athletes: A Cross-Sectional Study.
abstract: Objective: Female athletes have a higher prevalence of menstrual disorders due to hormonal imbalances, often related to physical stress, low energy availability, and inadequate nutritional habits. These disorders can affect both health and athletic performance. The aim of this study is to evaluate the frequency of menstrual cycle disorders in female athletes and their relationship with nutritional variables. Design: Observational, descriptive, cross-sectional study based on an anonymous online questionnaire administered to female athletes aged 18-55 years (n = 418; average age = 28 ± 9 years). Methods: The questionnaire collected self-reported data on menstrual cycle characteristics, diet, supplementation, and training-related habits. Chi-square tests, Fisher's exact test, and Kruskal-Wallis tests were used for statistical analysis, with significance set at p < 0.05. Results: Premenstrual symptoms were reported by 57.0% of participants, regular clot presence by 27.4%, and cycle irregularities by 22.8%. In unadjusted analyses, self-reported dietary balance was associated with cycle regularity and bleeding duration; after false discovery rate correction, only the association with altered bleeding duration (binary coding) remained statistically significant. No clear associations were observed between sports frequency and menstrual cycle alterations. Conclusions: Menstrual disorders were common among female athletes. Although an association between self-reported dietary balance and bleeding duration persisted after correction for multiple comparisons, it derived from an exploratory binary recoding and warrants cautious interpretation. These findings may help guide future research on nutrition and menstrual health in female athletes.

title: Intermittent Local Muscle Vibration Produces Smaller Knee Joint Position Sense Errors than Continuous Vibration: A Randomized Crossover Study in Knee Osteoarthritis.
abstract: This randomized crossover study compared immediate responses to different local muscle vibration protocols in 40 adults with knee osteoarthritis. Participants were randomized 1:1 to receive intermittent or continuous vibration first, then crossed over to the alternative protocol after washout. Vibration targeted the vastus medialis during 120 s of sit-to-stand exercise. Intermittent vibration was delivered only during seated and standing holds, whereas continuous vibration was delivered throughout the exercise. Knee joint position sense (JPS) errors were assessed at 20°, 40°, and 60° of flexion using inertial measurement units. Near-infrared spectroscopy recorded prefrontal and muscle hemodynamic responses during JPS testing. Assessments were performed at baseline and after each protocol. Data were analyzed using repeated-measures analysis of variance. Intermittent vibration produced smaller JPS errors than continuous vibration at all angles (1.96° versus 2.87°, 2.17° versus 3.20°, and 2.78° versus 4.72°, respectively, all p ≤ 0.019). Intermittent vibration elicited smaller changes in prefrontal total hemoglobin (0.23 versus 0.66 μM, p < 0.001), muscle oxygenated hemoglobin (2.32 versus 5.53 μM, p = 0.003), and muscle total hemoglobin (2.59 versus 6.13 μM, p = 0.004). Intermittent local muscle vibration produced smaller immediate knee JPS errors, whereas continuous vibration elicited larger hemodynamic responses.

title: Ramp lesions repaired during anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction are associated with similar functional outcomes to other medial meniscal lesions at 1 year: A prospective registry-based study.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate 12-month outcomes after primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) in patients with repaired ramp lesions compared with patients with other medial meniscal lesions or no meniscal lesions.
METHODS: This prospective registry-based study included patients undergoing primary ACLR with 12-month follow-up. Three propensity-score-matched comparisons were performed: ramp versus other medial meniscal lesions (94 vs. 94), ramp versus no meniscal lesions (107 vs. 205), and other medial meniscal lesions versus no meniscal lesions (103 vs. 103). Outcomes included knee function, psychological readiness, satisfaction and return to sport and work. Patient acceptable symptom state (PASS) and minimal clinically important difference (MCID) were defined as International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) scores ≥75.9 and improvements ≥10.7 points, respectively.
RESULTS: Among 110 patients with ramp lesions (60.9% male; mean age, 25.9 ± 8.9 years), knee function improved significantly at 12 months (p < 0.001). Postoperative IKDC scores did not differ significantly between ramp lesions and other medial meniscal lesions (86.6 vs. 84.5; p = 0.83) or no meniscal lesions (86.6 vs. 87.6; p = 0.15). However, compared with patients without meniscal lesions, those with ramp lesions reported lower subjective knee values (85.0 vs. 90.0; p = 0.007), psychological readiness (67.0 vs. 76.5; p = 0.02) and satisfaction (77.6% vs. 89.3%; p = 0.009). No significant differences were observed between other medial meniscal lesions and no meniscal lesions.
CONCLUSIONS: Repaired ramp lesions were associated with comparable functional outcomes but lower psychological readiness and satisfaction compared with isolated ACLR at 12 months, emphasizing the importance of patient-perceived recovery.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Warning signs of Injury: Changes in pain, training load, and wellness in elite youth athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Examine week-by-week changes during the four weeks preceding injury compared with injury-free weeks.
DESIGN: Prospective study.
SETTING: and main outcome: Training load was calculated as (weekly training minutes x average weekly rate of perceived exertion)/1000 (sRPE). Pain was assessed with a rating scale 0-10. Wellness (sleep, fatigue, stress and mental recovery) were standardized using Z-scores. Injury was self-reported.
PARTICIPANTS: Elite youth athletes.
RESULTS: Among 146 athletes, 118 (80.8%) reported 125 injuries. Mean age was 17.0 (SD 0.8). Compared with injury-free weeks, significantly higher pain scores were observed one (md [IQR]: 2.0 [0.0-4.0], p = 0.039) and two weeks (2.0 [1.0-3.0], p = 0.047) prior to injury. Median sRPE was significantly lower three (md [IQR]: 2.30 [0.75-4.20], p = 0.012) and four weeks (2.40 [0.96-3.96], p = 0.011). Sleep, stress and total wellness were significantly lower one week (mean [SD]: -0.348 [1.1], p = 0.004; -0.272 [0.9], p = 0.017; -0.244 [1.0], p = 0.011), while stress also showed reduction two weeks prior to injury (-0.244 [1.0], p = 0.042).
CONCLUSION: Changes were observed mainly in the week preceding injury. Increased pain and reduced wellness may serve as early warning signs, while decreased training load may reflect adaptation rather than causation. These findings support injury as a progressive process with detectable warning signs.

title: sEMG-IMU Fusion with Transfer Learning for Knee Flexion and Adduction Moment Estimation During Tai Chi.
abstract: Knee flexion moment (KFM) and knee adduction moment (KAM) are important indicators for assessing knee joint loading in patients with knee osteoarthritis (KOA). Tai Chi is commonly used as an exercise-based rehabilitation intervention for KOA, and accurate assessment of knee joint moments during Tai Chi is important for rehabilitation training. However, due to individual and cohort-related differences, the performance of knee joint moment prediction models often decreases markedly in cross-subject and cross-population applications. To address this issue, this study proposes a knee joint moment prediction method based on surface electromyography (sEMG) and inertial measurement unit (IMU) signals combined with transfer learning. sEMG and IMU data were collected from healthy participants and patients with KOA while performing multiple Tai Chi movements. A multimodal CNN-BiLSTM regression model was developed to simultaneously predict KFM and KAM, and three transfer learning strategies were designed for target-domain adaptation. The results showed that, under the more stringent repetition-level within-subject evaluation, the mean R2 values for KFM and KAM were 0.876 and 0.628, respectively, in the healthy group, and 0.750 and 0.651, respectively, in the KOA group. Direct prediction results in the cross-subject and cross-population tasks indicated substantial domain shifts across individuals and populations. Target-domain fine-tuning substantially improved prediction performance relative to direct prediction. In the transfer from healthy participants to patients with KOA, the R2 values for KFM and KAM increased from -0.627 and -0.138 under direct prediction to 0.660 and 0.497, respectively. However, target-only scratch training achieved R2 values of 0.687 and 0.574, indicating no additional benefit from healthy-source pretraining under the present protocol.

title: Chinese ethnic traditional sports as mind-body interventions for psychiatric recovery.
abstract: Chinese ethnic traditional sports (CETS)-a family of culturally embedded physical practices encompassing traditional Chinese mind-body exercises (e.g., Tai Chi, Qigong, Baduanjin, Yijin Jing, Wuqinxi) and intangible cultural heritage folk sports (e.g., dragon-lion dance)-have attracted growing interest as accessible, low-cost mind-body interventions for mental health. This narrative review examines which mental health outcomes are associated with participation in different types of CETS and to what extent the available evidence supports their role in psychiatric recovery. The review synthesizes 68 studies published between January 2000 and June 2026, identified through multi-database searches of Web of Science, PubMed, and Scopus. Thematic synthesis identified four interconnected dimensions of mental health burden addressed by CETS: (a) affective disorders; (b) trauma-related disorders; (c) sleep-wake disturbances; and (d) cognitive and psychosocial dysfunction. Across these dimensions, individual randomized controlled trials consistently report moderate reductions in depressive and anxiety symptoms, with larger effects when CETS are delivered in supervised groups at moderate intensity for 12-24 weeks; however, most evidence derives from subclinical or non-psychiatric samples and measures symptom severity rather than functional recovery. The review therefore concludes that CETS are a promising, low-cost, culturally congruent adjunct to conventional psychiatric care-warranting rigorous, disorder-specific trials-rather than established stand-alone treatments for psychiatric recovery.

title: Effects of Morning Strength and Power Priming Exercises on Afternoon Physical and Cognitive Performance in Male Rugby Union Players.
abstract: The objective of this study was to assess the effect of morning strength and power priming exercises on afternoon physical and cognitive performance in male rugby union players. On two occasions in a randomised, counterbalanced design, 25 male rugby union players completed morning physical (countermovement jump, 40 m linear sprint) and cognitive (rapid visual information processing; spatial working memory; paired associates of learning) assessments. Control (passive rest) or intervention (barbell back squat, 3 × 3 repetitions at 85% of one repetition maximum and barbell squat jump, 5 × 3 repetitions at 40% one repetition maximum) trials were implemented 5.5 h before afternoon assessments. Differences between morning and afternoon assessments were found in sprinting performance following intervention for 30 m fly (-0.08 ± 0.13 s, p = 0.004, ES: 0.615) and 40 m (-0.12 ± 0.17 s, p = 0.001, ES: 0.711) relative to control (0.03 ± 0.07 s, p = 0.022, ES: -0.476; 0.01 ± 0.09 s, p = 0.740, ES: -0.065, 30 m fly and 40 m, respectively). Afternoon countermovement jump flight time improved following intervention compared with control (2% vs. 0%, p = 0.012, ES: -0.53). No changes were found for cognitive assessments (p > 0.05). Morning strength and power priming exercises combining heavy-load traditional and light-load ballistic exercises effectively enhanced vertical jump and sprint performance, but not cognitive performance, in the afternoon in male rugby union players.

title: Home-based transcranial direct current stimulation and exercise for pain in people with knee osteoarthritis: A mixed-methods pilot randomised controlled trial.
abstract: This mixed-methods pilot trial evaluated the feasibility and patient perceptions of home-based transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) combined with exercise for pain in people with knee osteoarthritis. Twenty-four participants were allocated to active or sham home-based tDCS plus exercise. Participants completed 10 tDCS sessions over two weeks and an eight-week exercise program, with laboratory assessments at baseline, week four, and week eight. Primary outcomes were recruitment, adherence, adverse events, attrition, and tolerability. Secondary outcomes included local pressure pain thresholds, pain, function, quality of life, and semi-structured interviews exploring intervention facilitators and barriers. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively and qualitative data using inductive thematic analysis. All prespecified feasibility and safety criteria were met. Adherence was high, with 88% of participants (21/24) completing at least 75% of tDCS sessions, and 75% (18/24) completing at least 75% of exercise sessions. No significant adverse events occurred. Mean (SD) pain intensity /100 decreased from 47.3 (25.6) to 28.3 (16.1) in the active group and from 46.4 (17.8) to 33.5 (16.7) in the sham group at week 8. A future trial would require 80 participants. Qualitative themes indicated that evidence of effectiveness was more important to engagement than financial cost, tDCS was viewed as an appealing alternative to pharmacological treatment, and initial device operation was a greater barrier than safety or home use. Home-based tDCS combined with exercise was feasible, acceptable, and well tolerated. These findings support a fully powered trial to determine whether this scalable intervention improves pain and function in people with knee osteoarthritis. PERSPECTIVE: This pilot trial indicates that home-based tDCS combined with exercise is feasible, acceptable, and well tolerated for knee osteoarthritis. Participants valued its convenience and non-pharmacological nature. These findings support a fully powered trial to determine whether this scalable approach improves pain and function and broadens access to care.

title: Association Between Collision Exposure and Post-Match Physiological Recovery Markers in Rugby Union Players: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Background: Collision exposure during rugby union matches may influence post-match fatigue and recovery. However, direct evidence linking quantified match-related collision exposure to post-match recovery outcomes is limited. Objective: To systematically review associations between match-related collision exposure and post-match recovery outcomes in rugby union players and distinguish direct evidence from indirect or contextual evidence within the broader review framework. Methods: This review, registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF), followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement. PubMed and Scopus were searched (final search: 5 August 2026), with PubMed Central used for full-text retrieval. Studies of rugby union players were eligible, and the direct-evidence studies were all match-based studies in male players from professional or elite amateur settings. Among 605 records identified, 11 studies were retained within the review framework: 4 as direct evidence and 7 as indirect or contextual evidence. Owing to differences in collision exposure definitions, biomarkers, post-match assessment times, and effect measures, evidence was synthesized narratively according to the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis guideline. Results: Four match-based studies (79 enrolled players in total) provided direct evidence for the review question. Three examined biochemical markers associated with muscle damage, specifically creatine kinase, myoglobin, and interstitial creatine kinase, but they differed in collision metrics, specimen types, and post-match sampling windows, which ranged from 30-45 min to 24 and 40 h. Across these studies, higher collision exposure was generally associated with greater post-match perturbation in these muscle-damage-related biochemical responses, although the clearest reported association in Jones et al. was limited to backs and the statistical detail available from Smart et al. was comparatively limited. One small study suggested that greater collision frequency was associated with poorer post-match sleep architecture; however, this finding should be interpreted as preliminary single-study evidence for a recovery-related outcome rather than an established physiological trend. Direct evidence regarding neuromuscular fatigue was insufficient. One indirect study reported increased post-match resting metabolic rate but did not examine its association with quantified collision exposure. Conclusions: Limited direct evidence links collision exposure to post-match recovery-related outcomes. The strongest signal concerns muscle-damage-associated biochemical markers, but this evidence is based on only three heterogeneous studies with limited cross-study comparability. Evidence concerning sleep architecture remains preliminary and is currently based on a single small study. These findings are correlational. Hence, future match-based studies should separate collision exposure from other workload measures and assess recovery-related outcomes across domains at standardized post-match time points.

title: Effects of different exercise and ischemic preconditioning strategies on muscle damage after low-load blood flow restriction exercise: A randomized controlled trial.
abstract: Originally developed to protect against ischemia-reperfusion injury, ischemic preconditioning (IPC) may also attenuate exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) after eccentric exercise. Blood flow restriction resistance training (BFR-RT) combines contractions under restricted perfusion with reperfusion, but whether IPC before BFR-RT protects against EIMD is unknown. This trial tested whether preconditioning before BFR-RT attenuates EIMD. Forty participants were randomized to no preconditioning (CON), low-load exercise without BFR (LL), low-load exercise with BFR at 50% arterial occlusion pressure (AOP) (LL-BFR), or IPC with three 5-min occlusions at 100% AOP and 5-min reperfusion. Fifteen minutes later, participants performed four sets of knee extensions to concentric failure at 30% one repetition maximum (1RM) and 50% AOP. Isometric, concentric, and eccentric peak torque (PT) were assessed through 72 h alongside creatine kinase, myoglobin, muscle soreness, and muscle thickness. No Group × Time interactions occurred for PT (all p ≥ .716). At 24 h, isometric, concentric, and eccentric PT were reduced by 6.69%, 8.10%, and 6.89%, respectively. Eccentric and isometric PT recovered by 48 h, whereas concentric PT remained reduced by 3.92% at 72 h. Markers showed small changes without group differences. None of the preconditioning strategies blunted EIMD. Despite mechanistic overlap between IPC and BFR-RT, the mild to moderate damage response may limit measurable preconditioning effects.

title: Task Force 9: Clinical Considerations for the Care of Athletes with Cardiac Channelopathies.
abstract: Cardiac channelopathies, including long QT syndrome, catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, Brugada syndrome, and short QT syndrome, are heterogeneous conditions, which can lead to varying risks in athletes depending on their symptoms, disease severity, genotype, and therapies initiated. Historically, athletes with these conditions were excluded from participation with blanket restrictions, despite an absence of data. More recently, a number of studies have provided more scientific evidence to guide decision making and have been incorporated into these guidelines for athletes with cardiac channelopathies. Many athletes with these conditions may be supported in their decision to return to play as part of a shared decision-making model when they have been assessed, risk stratified, and appropriately treated by a specialist with expertise in these conditions.

title: Task Force 5: Clinical Considerations for Myocarditis and Selected Cardiovascular Conditions, Including Valvular Heart Disease.
abstract: Athletes with myocarditis, pericarditis, valvular heart disease, and other acquired cardiovascular conditions require careful evaluation when considering competitive sports participation. This document outlines key clinical considerations, risk factors, and expert consensus, serving as the rationale for Section V of the recent AHA/ACC Scientific Statement: Clinical Considerations for Competitive Sports Participation for Athletes with Cardiovascular Abnormalities. Disease-specific risk stratification and shared decision-making are essential in determining return-to-play eligibility. This Task Force document addresses myocarditis, pericarditis, the cardiovascular impact of respiratory viral infections, incidental myocardial fibrosis, Kawasaki disease, infiltrative cardiomyopathies, and valvular heart disease.

title: Dyslipidemia management in athletes: A comparative commentary on the 2026 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Guideline and contemporary sports cardiology recommendations.
abstract: Coronary artery disease (CAD) is the leading cause of exercise-related sudden cardiac death in athletes older than 35 years, and dyslipidemia is one of its principal modifiable drivers. The 2026 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Guideline on the Management of Blood Cholesterol introduces several advances directly relevant to athletes, including restored LDL-C treatment targets, universal lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] measurement, the PREVENT-ASCVD risk equations, expanded options for selective coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring, and a more aggressive approach to lipid-lowering therapy (LLT). However, sports cardiology guidelines and consensus statements offer important caveats that must be reconciled with these general-population recommendations: existing risk calculators, including PREVENT, do not reliably estimate cardiovascular risk in athletes, and routine CAC scoring is not recommended in athletes at low calculated risk. This commentary compares and contrasts general-population dyslipidemia recommendations with athlete-specific guidance from contemporary sports cardiology consensus documents, highlights recent evidence on Lp(a), wearable-derived training load, and risk score performance across the physical activity spectrum, and proposes a five-step clinical framework, refined to reflect athlete-specific risk stratification, for dyslipidemia evaluation and management in this population.

title: Functional asymmetry in elite female volleyball players: Crossover step blocking landing strategies quantified by symmetry angles.
abstract:
PURPOSE: The cross-step block is a key volleyball skill for stopping opponent attacks, yet it places substantial mechanical demands on the lower limbs during landing. This study compared lower-limb biomechanics and inter-limb symmetry between elite and sub-elite female volleyball players during rightward cross-step block landings.
METHODS: Thirty-two female players participated in the study: 16 elite and 16 sub-elite athletes. Three-dimensional kinematics and kinetics during the landing buffering phase were analyzed using two-way repeated-measures ANOVA and one-dimensional statistical parametric mapping (SPM1D). Inter-limb symmetry of discrete variables was evaluated using the Symmetry Angle (SA).
RESULTS: Elite players showed greater ankle dorsiflexion and knee flexion during landing than sub-elite players. A significant group-by-side interaction was observed for ankle transverse-plane motion, with the elite group showing greater external rotation on the right side. In addition, elite players exhibited larger positive SA values for ankle sagittal-plane moments, indicating greater right-side loading in the dominant limb. By contrast, sub-elite players showed smaller kinetic asymmetry but also lower joint excursion and lower energy-attenuation capacity.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that elite female volleyball players use a task-specific asymmetric landing strategy characterized by deep cushioning and dominant-limb braking. Training should emphasize eccentric control, unilateral ankle strength, and multi-planar landing stability to reduce overload risk while maintaining sport-specific performance.

title: Evidence and Gaps in Rehabilitation Activation of Piezoelectric Nanomaterials for Musculoskeletal Repair.
abstract: Prescribed rehabilitation may activate piezoelectric nanomaterials, but exercise-associated repair, exercise-induced electrical generation, and an independent electrical benefit require different evidence. This targeted narrative review evaluates these propositions in cartilage, bone, tendon and enthesis, and skeletal muscle. Primary studies were classified by prescribed exercise, spontaneous physiological loading, external ultrasound, or bench activation, and by whether they measured electrical exposure, structural repair, biomechanics, or behavior. Rabbit cartilage and rat tendon-to-bone studies provide exercise-associated proof of concept; they do not establish a reproducible in vivo electrical dose or durable functional recovery. Ultrasound studies support electromechanical plausibility under a different trigger, while bone and muscle evidence has limited direct rehabilitation relevance. Fiber alignment, particle dispersion, and scaffold geometry influence local deformation and charge generation, but also change mechanics and cell interactions. Calcium-dependent endogenous TGF-β signaling has been reported in specific PLLA systems; general ion-channel and integrin-FAK/YAP/TAZ pathways cannot be assigned to every piezoelectric construct. We propose an assessment pathway linking activity, implant strain, wet-state electrical exposure, biological response, and independently measured function. This pathway identifies missing measurements and controls rather than providing a calibrated dose-conversion rule. Prospective validation, matched inactive scaffolds, fatigue and release measurements, and functional outcomes are needed before clinical rehabilitation dosing can be justified.

title: Pediatric flexor tendon injuries: A 13-year retrospective review of injury characteristics, treatment, and outcomes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pediatric flexor tendon injuries are rare but potentially devastating. Due to low incidence, optimal perioperative management remains poorly defined, and evidence is scarce. This study evaluates the injury characteristics, surgical treatment, age-specific functional outcomes, and challenges in this population.
METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted on 79 pediatric patients (mean age 6.84 ± 4.27 years; 67.1% male) who underwent surgical repair for flexor tendon lacerations between 2010 and 2023. Outcomes were assessed using Total Active Motion (TAM), Strickland score, grip/pinch strength, Semmes-Weinstein monofilament, two-point discrimination, and QuickDASH questionnaire, with a mean follow-up of 59.9 ± 32.8 months.
RESULTS: Zone 2 was the most common injury site (45.6%), with glass being the predominant mechanism (67.1%). Nerve injury was present in 35.4% of cases. Overall, good/excellent results were achieved in 81.9% (TAM) and 89.0% (Strickland) of patients. The 0-5 years age group had significantly lower Strickland scores than the 6-12 years group (74.28% vs. 82.9%, p < 0.05). Zone 5 injuries demonstrated significantly better outcomes than Zone 2 and 3 (p < 0.001). The overall complication rate was low (5.1%), with a rerupture rate of 2.5%.
CONCLUSION: Pediatric flexor tendon repairs yield favorable functional outcomes with low complication rates. Age-related differences in functional outcomes should be interpreted cautiously because of developmental differences in patient cooperation and age-dependent rehabilitation strategies. Concomitant nerve injury was associated with poorer functional outcomes. The modified Kessler technique remains a reliable repair method.

title: Increases in Agility and Quantitative Movement Quality Following a Coach-Led, Basketball-Specific Neuromuscular Training Warm-Up Programme in Adolescent Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Coach-led, basketball-specific neuromuscular training (NMT) warm-up programs have been shown to reduce injury risk. However, changes in agility and movement quality following such NMT in high school basketball players are not well characterized.
METHODS: In this pre-experimental study, high school basketball players (42 males, 31 females, 16 ± 1.4 years) performed a 10-minute, coach-led, basketball-specific NMT warm-up programme before practices and games (10-14 weeks). Changes in the Lane Agility Test (LAT) and single-leg squat (SLS) kinematics, encompassing trunk, pelvis, hip, and lower extremity kinematics and a composite score (SLS Score), from pre-to post-intervention were assessed. Relationships between pre-intervention scores, sex, the number of NMT sessions completed, and outcomes were assessed with linear regressions.
RESULTS: LAT completion times decreased following the NMT intervention, with larger changes associated with slower pre-intervention scores and more completed NMT sessions. SLS Scores were higher after the NMT intervention, potentially attributable to better pelvic and hip kinematics.
CONCLUSIONS: In this single-arm preliminary and exploratory study, favourable changes in agility and SLS kinematics following a coach-led, basketball-specific NMT programme were observed, with preliminary evidence of a dose-response relationship for agility. However, this study was non-randomized and lacked a control group. Therefore, these results should not be interpreted to suggest a causal relationship between the NMT performed and the changes in outcomes. In addition to NMT's role in injury prevention, coaches and players should be cognizant about performance and movement quality changes potentially associated with this accessible version of NMT.

title: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport and its Implications for the Foot and Ankle Surgeon.
abstract: Relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) is a syndrome caused by low energy availability that affects multiple physiologic systems in both male and female athletes. Stress fractures of the foot and ankle are often the first signs of RED-S; therefore, it is crucial that orthopedic surgeons are aware of and able to identify this disorder. This article focuses on RED-S and provides a framework for understanding the disorder, it's relevancy to the orthopedic foot and ankle surgeon, and offers suggestions for diagnostic strategies and treatment approaches that are imperative for safe return to play.

title: Vitamin D Insufficiency as a Nutritional Stress Amplifier: An Evidence-Weighted Framework for Adaptive Reserve under Exercise and Energy-Deficit Stress.
abstract: Vitamin D is a fat-soluble secosteroid whose biological activity depends on conversion of circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D into calcitriol, the active ligand of the vitamin D receptor. Although vitamin D has often been discussed as a potential ergogenic nutrient, evidence for direct performance-enhancing effects in athletes remains inconsistent. This review proposes that vitamin D insufficiency, used here as a context-dependent descriptive label for low circulating 25(OH)D rather than as a universal diagnostic category, may function as a nutritional stress amplifier that narrows adaptive reserve when mechanical, energetic, endocrine, inflammatory, and neuroendocrine stressors converge. The strongest evidence derives from the vitamin D-calcium-phosphate-PTH-FGF23 axis, through which calcitriol-VDR signaling supports mineral homeostasis, skeletal remodeling, and resilience to repetitive skeletal loading. Emerging evidence suggests intersections with skeletal muscle repair, myokine and osteokine signaling, inflammatory regulation, and tissue adaptation, although athlete-specific validation is needed. Low energy availability and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport provide a translational model in which low circulating 25(OH)D may become more relevant because multiple nutritional, endocrine, skeletal, and recovery stressors coexist. Brain-related pathways involving fatigue, sleep, HPA-axis-related recovery, BDNF, monoaminergic signaling, and interoceptive processing are retained only as hypothesis-generating domains, not as evidence that vitamin D status modifies cognition, mood, motivation, behavior, or central recovery mechanisms in athletes. Future studies should move beyond static 25-hydroxyvitamin D assessment and unstratified supplementation trials toward dynamic stress-recovery phenotyping. This framework positions low circulating 25(OH)D status as a testable conditional modifier of stress-recovery trajectories rather than an isolated determinant of athletic performance or a primary clinical target.

title: Arthrogenic muscle inhibition and quadriceps activation failure after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: Early assessment and rehabilitation beyond strength.
abstract: Arthrogenic muscle inhibition (AMI) is common in the early postoperative period after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) and can persist throughout rehabilitation. However, clinically assessing AMI is challenging, typically requiring muscle stimulation-based testing with dynamometry and/or electromyography (EMG) to estimate the precise degree of quadriceps activation failure. However, a reliable clinical examination can identify and grade the overt contraction impairment, extension loss and hamstring contracture often associated with laboratory assayed AMI. A recent report found 49% of patients at 3 weeks and 24% at 6 weeks after ACLR present with at least one clinically detectable sign of likely AMI. Preoperative clinical AMI, greater immediate postoperative pain and absence of preoperative physiotherapy were associated with higher prevalence of clinical AMI at 3 weeks, highlighting the vital nature of early physiotherapy and pain management. As the patient progresses, since AMI refers to the neural inhibition of the muscle secondary to joint injury, strength gains can actually coexist with persistent activation deficits. Thus, traditional strengthening programs may not be achieving optimal efficiency when attempting to restore strength after joint injury. Rehabilitation that integrates activation exercises, symptom management and progressive strengthening, with neuromuscular electrical stimulation and/or biofeedback may reduce AMI and enhance recovery. At return to sport, strength recovery should not be interpreted as proof of activation recovery and specialised muscle activation testing should be considered selectively when clinical testing is inconclusive. Future studies should determine whether identifying and treating activation deficits improves functional recovery and informs safer return-to-sport decisions.

title: Global Perspective in Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction in Soccer Players: Current Concepts for the 2026 World Cup.
abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament injuries in soccer players represent a major challenge in modern sports medicine, particularly among elite athletes. Despite significant advances in surgical techniques, graft biology, and rehabilitation protocols graft failure rates, reinjury, and suboptimal return-to-sport outcomes remain clinically relevant concerns. Contemporary approaches emphasize a multifactorial strategy encompassing injury prevention, individualized graft selection, restoration of rotational and multiplanar stability, meniscal preservation, and criteria-based return-to-sport progression. Data from global registries and patient groups show that graft failure rates approach 10% for all types of grafts. This highlights the importance of a more holistic surgical approach that addresses the entire knee rather than focusing solely on replacing individual ligaments. There is growing evidence that adding lateral extra-articular procedures reduces failure rates, especially in high-risk athletes such as soccer players where cutting and pivoting are common. It is also crucial to recognize and treat concomitant injuries including meniscal tears, posterior meniscal root injuries, and medial instability to improve long-term outcomes. It is important to provide a comprehensive overview of anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in soccer players, integrating insights from an international symposium held in 2026 with the latest evidence available. Key areas covered include injury prevention strategies, biomechanics of injuries, graft selection, restoration of rotational stability, meniscal function preservation, rehabilitation approaches, and future directions for personalized medicine.

title: Sports-Related Back Pain and Injuries: From Muscle Strain to Spondylolisthesis.
abstract: Back pain is common in both the general population and young athletes, with risk increasing in sports that involve repetitive extension, rotation, and axial loading. Although most cases resolve with time, accurate diagnosis is essential to distinguish common musculoskeletal causes from more serious conditions. This article reviews key causes of athletic back pain, including muscle strain, mechanical low back pain, spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis, lumbar disc herniation, and sacroiliac joint dysfunction. It also examines diagnosis, treatment, and return to play considerations. Early recognition and appropriate management help ensure a safe and timely return to sport.

title: Performance-Centred Weight Management: A Harm-Reduction Framework for Emerging Body Mass Interventions in Sport.
abstract: Highly effective incretin-based therapies are increasingly extending beyond obesity treatment into fitness, body image, and sporting environments, raising new questions regarding athletes' health, informed decision-making, performance enhancement, and off-label use. Direct extrapolation of evidence from obesity medicine to athletes is inappropriate because body mass management in sport must preserve training adaptation and physiological readiness for competition. This Perspective proposes Performance-Centred Weight Management (PCWM), a health-oriented conceptual framework intended to guide the evaluation of traditional weight-cutting practices, nutritional interventions, structured exercise programmes, incretin-based therapies, and future body mass interventions in sport. PCWM integrates five interdependent domains: muscle quality and function, energy availability, recovery and training adaptation, sport-specific performance capacity, and long-term athlete health and wellbeing, within a model of longitudinal monitoring aligned with training periodisation. PCWM distinguishes evaluation from endorsement. Rather than considering body mass reduction as the primary endpoint, the framework identifies physiological readiness for competition, athlete health, and informed decision-making as the principal outcomes of successful body mass management. By integrating performance-oriented assessment with medical supervision and harm-minimisation principles, PCWM offers a conceptual basis for evaluating emerging pharmacological body mass interventions. However, the framework has not yet undergone empirical validation, and its feasibility, clinical utility, and applicability across sporting disciplines require further investigation. Future research should examine off-label use, access pathways, risk perception, sport-specific physiological outcomes, and potential interactions between pharmacological appetite suppression, low energy availability, and training adaptation.

title: Clinical Assessments to Inform Return to Play Prognosis Following Acute Hamstring Injury: An Evidence-Informed Guide for Clinicians.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Rehabilitation clinicians aim to provide a return to play (RTP) prognosis following acute hamstring injury based on various clinical assessments, including subjective interview questions and physical examinations. CLINICAL QUESTION: What subjective interview questions and physical examinations should be prioritised during an initial clinical assessment following acute hamstring injury to inform RTP? KEY RESULTS: There are key subjective interview questions and physical examination findings to inform RTP prognosis following acute hamstring injury. Prolonged RTP time has been associated with athletes who: 1) recall higher pain ratings at the time of injury; 2) report pain with palpation closer to the ischial tuberosity; 3) have greater cranio-caudal length of palpable pain; 4) present with between-leg deficits of greater magnitude in maximal hip flexion active knee extension range of motion and isometric knee flexion strength in outer-range (supine with 90° hip/knee flexion) and/or mid-range (prone with 0° hip and ~15° knee flexion); and 4) experience pain during outer-range hamstring contraction. CLINICAL APPLICATION: This evidence-informed clinical commentary may help clinicians prioritise subjective interview questions and physical examinations to inform their RTP prognosis following acute hamstring injury.

title: Arthrogenic Muscle Inhibition and Quadriceps Dysfunction After Primary and Revision Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) reliably relieves pain in end-stage knee osteoarthritis, but quadriceps dysfunction may continue to limit walking, stair climbing, balance, and confidence. This narrative review examines arthrogenic muscle inhibition (AMI) and quadriceps dysfunction after primary and revision TKA. PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception through August 2026 using terms related to AMI, quadriceps activation, TKA, and rehabilitation. Relevant studies were selected for narrative synthesis, prioritizing direct TKA evidence and identifying evidence from other knee populations as indirect. AMI is impaired voluntary activation associated with altered joint afferent input and neural inhibition, whereas atrophy reflects loss of muscle tissue. Both can coexist and contribute to weakness. Surgical trauma, pain, effusion, inflammation, altered proprioception, and immobilization may impair early motor-unit recruitment. Preoperative weakness, inactivity, obesity, comorbidity, and revision surgery may further reduce physiological reserve. Muscle-preserving exposure may improve selected early outcomes, but must not compromise safe exposure or component positioning. Revision procedures add tissue injury, extensor-mechanism risk, systemic illness, and rehabilitation restrictions; direct voluntary-activation evidence after revision TKA remains limited. Assessment should combine strength and functional testing with measures of voluntary activation and muscle morphology when feasible. Management includes pain and swelling control, safe early activation, progressive strengthening, neuromuscular electrical stimulation, selected blood-flow-restriction training, motor-control rehabilitation, and targeted prehabilitation. Nutritional and laboratory assessment can identify modifiable risks but does not diagnose AMI. A practical perioperative framework is proposed to support identification and management of quadriceps dysfunction after primary and revision TKA.

title: The knee replacement that never happened: a case of recovery following structured neuromuscular rehabilitation.
abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a common cause of pain and reduced mobility, often leading patients to consider total knee replacement (TKR). Exercise is recommended as part of treatment; however, there is little guidance on the optimal type or duration of rehabilitation before surgery. As a result, some patients may be listed for TKR before receiving a structured trial of nonoperative care. We report the case of a 78-year-old woman with symptomatic knee OA placed on a National Health Service waiting list for TKR. While awaiting surgery, she undertook the Awareness, Resistance, Individualized, Stability, and Essential OrthoPrehab programme, a structured neuromuscular rehabilitation programme focusing on joint awareness, movement control, proprioception, and strengthening. After 3 months, she experienced improvements in pain, function, and confidence, reduced reliance on analgesics, and withdrew from the surgical waiting list. This case highlights the potential of structured rehabilitation to help some patients avoid surgery.

title: Prevalence and associated factors of depression, anxiety, and stress among university athletes in Bangladesh.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: University athletes face substantial academic, physical, and psychosocial pressures that may heighten vulnerability to psychological distress, despite the perceived mental health benefits of sports participation. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of depression, anxiety, and stress among university athletes in Bangladesh and to examine how these conditions are associated with lifestyle and sociodemographic factors.
METHODS: This cross-sectional study was conducted from March to September 2025 among 249 university athletes aged 18-26 years at six randomly selected universities in Bangladesh. Data were collected online and in person. Psychological distress was assessed with the Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Scale-21 (DASS-21), and health-promoting lifestyle behaviors were evaluated with the Health-Promoting Lifestyle Profile II (HPLP-II). Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, Mann-Whitney U tests, Spearman's correlations, and binary logistic regression analyses were conducted.
RESULTS: The prevalence of depression, anxiety, and stress was 42.6%, 42.6%, and 43.8%, respectively. Depression, anxiety, and stress were significantly associated with relationship status, fatigue, socioeconomic status, smoking, sleep duration, sports participation frequency, and satisfaction with sports (all p < 0.05). Participants with depression, anxiety, and stress had significantly lower scores across all HPLP-II domains (all p < 0.01). Higher physical activity was independently associated with lower odds of depression (OR = 0.462, 95% CI: 0.286-0.746), anxiety (OR = 0.756, 95% CI: 0.677-0.845), and stress (OR = 0.773, 95% CI: 0.677-0.882). Better stress management and stronger interpersonal relationships were also significantly associated, whereas other factors were not.
CONCLUSIONS: Depression, anxiety, and stress were highly prevalent among university athletes in Bangladesh and strongly associated with modifiable lifestyle factors. These findings support integrated, athlete-centered mental health strategies emphasizing physical activity, stress management, and psychosocial support. However, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference and determination of the directionality of these associations.
CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.

title: Sex Differences in Psychological Traits, Training Volume, and Dietary Food-Frequency Patterns in Athletes: Associations with Body Dissatisfaction.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Psychological traits, training volume, and dietary behaviors have been associated with body-image and eating-related outcomes in athletes, but evidence integrating these domains from a sex-based perspective remains limited.
OBJECTIVES: This study examined sex differences in psychological traits, weekly training volume, and study-specific dietary food-frequency scores, and evaluated their associations with body dissatisfaction assessed using the Body Dissatisfaction subscale of the Eating Disorder Inventory (EDI).
METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted in 58 athletes (23 women and 35 men). Participants completed questionnaires assessing personality traits, psychological inflexibility, anxiety, loneliness, training characteristics, dietary food-frequency patterns, and body dissatisfaction. Weekly training volume was calculated as the sum of weekly minutes across three intensity zones (Z1 + Z2 + Z3). Analyses included descriptive statistics, Welch's t-tests, Pearson and Spearman correlations, and a hypothesis-driven multivariable ordinary least squares model.
RESULTS: Female athletes had higher EDI Body Dissatisfaction scores and neuroticism than male athletes. Female athletes also had a higher non-pro-inflammatory food-frequency score (22.83 ± 6.31 vs. 19.34 ± 5.50; p = 0.036), whereas the pro-inflammatory food-frequency score did not differ significantly by sex (p = 0.327). Weekly training volume did not differ by sex and was not significantly associated with body dissatisfaction within either sex. In the multivariable model, female sex (B = 2.615, p = 0.036) and the pro-inflammatory food-frequency score (B = 0.308, p = 0.048) were positively associated with EDI Body Dissatisfaction scores; BMI showed an imprecise positive estimate in both the primary and age-adjusted models, whereas neuroticism, weekly training volume, and the non-pro-inflammatory food-frequency score were not independently associated. Model fit was modest (adjusted R2 = 0.180; 5-fold cross-validated R2 = 0.058 ± 0.333).
CONCLUSIONS: Women in this sample reported greater body dissatisfaction and neuroticism. The association between the study-specific pro-inflammatory food-frequency score and body dissatisfaction was small and exploratory and should not be interpreted as evidence of a causal dietary effect or of biological inflammatory exposure. Larger studies with sport-type information, validated dietary indices, and objective training-load measures are required to test these associations.

title: Adaptive training load optimization for sprinters via offline reinforcement learning and multi-modal physiological feedback.
abstract: Elite sprint training requires daily adjustment of training load to balance performance adaptation and fatigue, yet physiological monitoring does not necessarily translate into a specific next-session prescription. This study formalizes daily sprint training prescription as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process and develops an adaptive load-optimization framework that couples multi-modal physiological feedback with offline reinforcement learning (RL). A 19-dimensional state fusing autonomic, neuromuscular, endocrine, subjective, and load-aggregate signals is encoded by a dual-tower network [a one-dimensional convolutional neural network-Transformer temporal branch and a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) static branch] over an action space of 62 admissible training-type/intensity/volume combinations. A composite reward penalizes overreaching while rewarding short-term gain, longitudinal adaptation, and acute-to-chronic workload ratio conformity. The policy is learned by conservative off-policy training on retrospective data, evaluated through the Fitted Q-Evaluation (FQE) and Doubly Robust (DR) estimators, and presented to coaches as the three leading candidate actions, with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values used to explain the model's preferences among the candidate actions. In a 12-week single-center retrospective comparison of 70 national-level sprinters (35 men and 35 women; 100 m personal best (PB) ≤ 11.20 s for men or ≤ 12.50 s for women), grouped by whether their squad had adopted the tool (n = 35 RL-guided) or continued classical block periodisation (n = 35 control), the RL-guided cohort demonstrated between-cohort differences of +0.240 s in 100 m [95% confidence interval (CI) +0.128 to +0.352; p < 0.001, d = 1.00], +0.104 s in 30 m (p < 0.001, d = 1.00) and +2.17 cm in countermovement jump (p < 0.001, d = 1.01). Zero algorithmically defined sustained multi-indicator fatigue/load events were observed in the RL-guided cohort vs. seven in the control cohort (1.43 per 1,000 athlete-days); these events should not be interpreted as clinically diagnosed overtraining syndrome. Off-policy evaluation yielded exploratory point estimates whose precision remains unknown because uncertainty intervals were not calculated. These observational findings describe associations with an RL-guided, coach-in-the-loop workflow and do not establish a causal effect of the RL policy.

title: Collective case study on periodized training in elite female middle- and long-distance swimmers preparing for national competition.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Elite swimmers increasingly face calendars requiring multiple performance peaks within a single season, a scenario for which traditional single-target periodization models may be insufficient.
METHODS: This longitudinal collective case study followed five elite female middle- and long-distance freestyle swimmers across a 52-week macrocycle preparing for two national championships. The program combined three altitude camps, sea-level integration phases and two timed tapers. Training intensity distribution (TID) was quantified with a three-zone lactate-threshold model; hemoglobin, hematocrit, red blood cell count, creatine kinase and cortisol were measured at four time points; and performance was assessed by time-trial and official competition results. Given N = 5, analysis prioritized a smallest-worthwhile-change (SWC) classification for performance and paired effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals for blood markers rather than null-hypothesis significance testing. Hematological outcomes are concentration-based indices; training-load descriptors refer to in-water swimming only.
RESULTS: Applying an SWC of ≈0.24% to the 20 athlete-by-event observations, 12/20 (60%) changes at Competition 1 and 18/20 (90%) at Competition 2 exceeded the SWC, most representing improvement over baseline; this ordering held across the full defensible range of reference variability (SWC 0.22-0.42%). Hematological effect sizes were largest at Week 27 (RBC: Hedges' g = 2.32, 95% CI [0.64, 4.01]; HCT: g = 2.04 [0.50, 3.58]), while creatine kinase and cortisol peaked at Week 17 and were closer to baseline at Week 49, compatible with a lower physiological stress state at that sampled time point. TID shifted across phases (pyramidal during base development, polarized during altitude blocks, threshold-oriented during race-pace sharpening), with marked inter-individual heterogeneity in performance and physiological responses.
CONCLUSION: Across this double-peak macrocycle, most athlete-by-event changes exceeded the SWC, and the proportion doing so was higher at the second championship than at the first; these changes occurred alongside altitude-associated increases in concentration-based oxygen-transport indices and a taper-associated normalization of creatine kinase and cortisol. With no control group or randomization, only five athletes and four blood samples, several simultaneous interventions and unmeasured confounders (iron status, menstrual-cycle phase, dryland load), these findings describe associations only. They are offered as exploratory, hypothesis-generating observations from a single elite squad rather than as causal evidence.

title: Smartphone Accelerometer Assessment of HRV: Concurrent Agreement of the KubiosHRV App.
abstract: Heart rate variability (HRV) is widely used to monitor athlete recovery and adaptation. Recent technological advances have enabled HRV assessment through smartphone applications without the need for external devices. This study aimed to assess the concurrent agreement between the accelerometer-based HRV measurement feature of the KubiosHRV app and the Polar H10 in supine, seated, and standing positions. A total of 52 participants (30 males and 22 females) across performance tiers 0-4 completed a 2 min resting recording, with the first minute discarded and the second minute analysed in each position. HRV was measured simultaneously using a Polar H10 chest strap and the accelerometer-based feature of the KubiosHRV app on an iPhone 14. The analysed variables included Mean RR, RMSSD, SDNN, LF power, HF power, SD1, and SD2. Data were automatically processed by the KubiosHRV app and manually extracted into a database. Results showed excellent intraclass correlation coefficients (≥0.985) and small magnitudes of error for time-domains and non-linear variables in the three analysed positions with the reference criterion. Frequency-domain variables showed larger error estimates. Bland-Altman analysis showed no evidence of proportional bias across the measurement range (p > 0.05). These findings suggest that, during 1 min recordings, the accelerometer-based feature of the KubiosHRV app showed strong concurrent agreement with the Polar H10 for time-domain variables and acceptable agreement for selected non-linear variables across positions. Therefore, it may represent a practical alternative for routine monitoring of these HRV metrics when external hardware is unavailable.

title: The Impact of Race-to-Race Fatigue on Performance in a 24-Hour Competitive Swimming Schedule.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To examine the sequence of physiological, perceptual, and neuromuscular responses to successive competitive events performed within 24 hours in U16 and U18 national-level swimmers and to determine whether cumulative fatigue impairs performance-related markers.
METHODS: Nineteen highly trained junior swimmers (11 males and 8 females; age 16 [1] y) competed in a "direct-final" format (no heats), completing at least 3 separate maximum-effort finals (50-400 m) during the first 24 hours of the Spanish National Championships. Swimmers were categorized by age: U16 and U18. Countermovement jump, blood lactate, heart rate, and rating of perceived exertion (RPE) were measured 15 minutes before and immediately after each of the 3 events. General linear models and linear mixed-effects models were employed to evaluate the changes over time, group differences (U16 vs U18), sex, and interactions effects. Effect sizes were reported as η2 or partial η2.
RESULTS: Blood lactate concentration increased significantly (P < .001) from prerace to postrace at each event, reaching a peak of 15.4 (4.7) mmol·L-1 in sprinters. U16 swimmers showed a higher cardiovascular response compared with U18 as the competition progressed (P = .002). The swim team achieved a historic sixth-place overall regional finish, with 37% of the athletes improving their personal bests. No sequential reductions were observed for countermovement jump, F(2,16) = 0.54, P = .593, which remained stable at ∼33 to 34 cm postrace for 50 to 100 m and ∼30 to 31 cm for 200- to 400-m finals, indicating preserved neuromuscular performance.
CONCLUSIONS: Although successive races induce substantial metabolic and cardiovascular stress, lower-limb explosive performance remains stable. Youth swimmers appear capable of tolerating congested multievent competition without substantial impairment in lower body neuromuscular power.

title: Open and closed-chain shoulder joint position sense: inter-day reliability and normative profiles in male contact sport athletes.
abstract: The purpose was to determine inter-day reliability and normative values for open and closed-chain shoulder joint position sense (JPS). Male contact and collision sport athletes (18-40 years) participated in two study phases. Sixteen athletes completed open- and closed-chain JPS tests on two occasions (2-9 days apart) to determine inter-day reliability. Twenty-eight athletes completed the same protocol on one occasion to establish normative profiles. Open-chain JPS was assessed in a standing position using shoulder flexion to pre-defined angles with a laser pointer (55°, 90° and 125° of humerothoracic flexion; no haptic target); closed-chain JPS was assessed in a push-up position by reproducing target positions (chest lowered onto a hurdle at 16.5 cm [low] or 30.5 cm [high]; an initial haptic target). Three-dimensional kinematics quantified repositioning errors. Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and standard error of measurement (SEM) were calculated for reliability. Pearson correlations were calculated between open and closed-chain errors. Open-chain tests demonstrated moderate reliability across both arms (ICCs = 0.71-0.74), with better reliability on the dominant limb (ICCs = 0.68-0.90) compared to the non-dominant (ICCs = 0.43-0.55). SEM values ranged from 0.70 to 2.03°. Closed-chain tests showed poor reliability at the high target (ICC = 0.49) but good reliability at the low target (ICC = 0.81, SEM = 10.2 mm). Normative data indicated greater repositioning errors at low targets in open-chain tasks and at high targets in closed-chain tasks. Correlations between open- and closed-chain errors were weak to absent. Open-chain JPS testing demonstrated acceptable reliability, whereas closed-chain reliability was dependent on target height. The two tasks appear to assess distinct aspects of proprioception. The open-chain test reflects predominantly single-joint (glenohumeral) position sense, whereas the closed-chain test reflects multi-joint, composite position sense. These findings establish initial reference values for JPS in male contact athletes.

title: Associations between countermovement jump impulse and running kinetics following ACL reconstruction.
abstract: Persistent deficits in lower-limb loading are commonly observed following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) and may influence running biomechanics. Countermovement jump (CMJ) impulse can provide a phase-specific measure of force-time characteristics to reflect limb loading capacity; however, its relationship with running kinetics remains unclear. This study aimed to quantify phase-specific CMJ impulse following ACLR and examine associations with vertical ground reaction force (vGRF) metrics during treadmill running at the return-to-running phase. Forty-two participants performed three unilateral and bilateral CMJs on dual force plates and ran at 8 km/hr on an instrumented treadmill. Concentric, eccentric braking, and landing impulses were calculated. Running variables included weight acceptance rate, weight acceptance peak force, and maximum applied force. Inter-limb differences were assessed using Wilcoxon/paired t-tests. Impulse-vGRF relationships were analysed using Pearson/Spearman correlations and multiple linear regression. The ACLR limb exhibited significant deficits across all unilateral and bilateral CMJ phases, except for unilateral landing impulse. Deficits were greatest for unilateral concentric impulse (Δ1.3Ns·kg-0.67, d = 1.49, p < 0.001). Maximum applied force limb symmetry index (LSI) was explained by unilateral concentric impulse LSI (adjusted R2 = 0.25, p < 0.001). Maximum applied force of the affected limb was explained by unilateral concentric impulse (adjusted R2 = 0.38, p < 0.001). Weight acceptance peak force of the affected limb was explained by unilateral concentric and landing impulses (adjusted R2 = 0.37, p < 0.001). No meaningful relationships were observed for eccentric impulses or weight acceptance rate metrics. These findings indicate that jump impulse testing may provide clinically relevant indicators of running kinetics.

title: Age- and maturation-related differences in the relationships between sport-specific agility, linear sprint, and vertical jump performance in young male soccer players.
abstract: Agility shows weaker associations with physical qualities in older compared with younger age groups of young athletes; however, these relationships have not yet been examined using ecologically valid agility tests. The aim of this study was to assess the age- and maturation-related differences in the relationships between agility, linear sprint, and vertical jump performance in young male soccer players, using an agility test with a soccer-specific human stimulus. Fifty-seven young male soccer players participated in the study, divided into two groups based on chronological age (U11/12 and U13/14) and estimated maturity status (Pre-PHV and Circa-PHV). Participants completed linear sprint tests (10-m, 20-m), a countermovement jump test (CMJ), and a soccer-specific human stimulus-based agility test. Significant correlations were observed between agility and 10-m (ρ = 0.468, P = 0.030; ρ = 0.386, P = 0.020) and 20-m sprint performance (ρ = 0.502, P = 0.021; ρ = 0.450, P = 0.006) in the U11/12 and Pre-PHV groups, respectively, whereas these correlations were nonsignificant in the U13/14 and Circa-PHV groups. However, formal comparisons revealed no significant differences in correlation magnitude between chronological age or maturity groups (P > 0.05). Nonsignificant correlations were found between agility and CMJ performance in all subgroups. Partial correlation analyses controlling for maturity offset attenuated all the observed associations in the total sample and in all subgroups. Overall, agility showed generally limited associations with linear sprint and vertical jump performance, with no evidence that the strength of these relationships differed systematically across the examined age or maturity groups.

title: Nationwide Trends, Regional Variation and Seasonality of Surgically Treated Achilles Tendon Rupture in Japan: An Analysis of Descriptive Epidemiological Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Achilles tendon rupture (ATR) is a common foot and ankle injury among physically active adults. Nationwide evidence on long-term trends, regional variation, seasonality and COVID-19-related changes in Japan is limited. We characterised the surgical burden of ATR using a national administrative database.
METHODS: We conducted a nationwide descriptive epidemiological study using aggregated data from the National Database of Health Insurance Claims and Specific Health Checkups (NDB) Open Data for fiscal years (FY) 2014-2022. Temporal trends, prefectural variation, seasonal patterns and pandemic-associated changes were examined using counts, population-based rates and quasi-Poisson regression.
RESULTS: During FY2014-2019, approximately 11,200 surgeries were performed annually (8.8 per 100,000 person). In FY2020, incidence declined to 5.9 per 100,000 (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 0.67), with greater reductions among adults aged 30-59 (61%-64% of baseline) and, after age adjustment, among women (IRR 0.61 vs. 0.71 in men; interaction p = 0.039). Incidence partially recovered in FY2021-2022 (7.6 per 100,000; IRR 0.86). Incidence varied across the 47 prefectures (pre-COVID range: 5.0-16.7 per 100,000), and all declined in FY2020 (mean ratio 0.69). Monthly counts peaked in spring-early summer and were higher in spring than in winter (p = 0.018).
CONCLUSIONS: The incidence of surgically treated ATR in Japan was stable before the COVID-19 pandemic, declined markedly in FY2020 and partially recovered thereafter, with the largest reductions among working-age adults and women. Regional variation and seasonality were preserved. These findings can inform surgical and rehabilitation service planning.

title: Time-Efficient Reactive Agility Training Improves Motor and Cognitive Components of Reactive Agility in Open- and Closed-Skill Athletes: A 6-Week Intervention Study.
abstract: Reactive agility (RA), the ability to respond to external stimuli with whole-body movements as quickly and precisely as possible, is crucial for many sports, particularly open-skill sports, and is influenced by both motor and cognitive abilities. This study aims to investigate which of the underlying components of RA is most improved through RA training, whether prior experience with RA movements influences the rate of improvement, and whether a time-ecological approach also leads to improvements. Assessments included 19 open-skill and 26 closed-skill athletes with different competitive backgrounds. RA training was carried out once a week for six weeks with each session lasting 20 minutes. Pre- and post-assessments were conducted for RA (Random Star Run), change-of-direction (t-Test), and cognitive performance (Stroop test). Baseline differences between open- and closed-skill athletes and performance level were evaluated using 2 × 2 ANOVA. Intervention effects were calculated using repeated measures ANOVA. Open-skill athletes were significantly faster within the RA task than closed-skill athletes (p = 0.017; F = 6.247; η2 p = 0.132). Both groups improved significantly across all outcome measures (p < 0.05; RA and both underlying properties) with no interaction effects of group × time (p > 0.05). One weekly 20-min training session is sufficient to improve RA, and selected motor and cognitive performance parameters. Prior experience, based on regular participation in open-skill sports, seems to be associated with higher RA performance but does not moderate training adaptations, as both groups improved similarly in RA and the underlying motor and cognitive functions.

title: Mechanisms and Movement Patterns of Ankle Sprain Injuries in Male Handball: A Video-Based Analysis.
abstract: Ankle sprains are among the most common injuries in handball. However, evidence on high-risk movements and injury circumstances is scarce. This video analysis study investigated the situational characteristics of athletes sustaining ankle sprains. A systematic web search (YouTube, Google News) identifying video recordings of ankle injuries in male handball players was performed. Two independent examiners extracted sample information (e.g., age, height, weight, position), mechanism of injury (direct, indirect, non-contact), movement pattern (landing, change of direction/CoD, running, shuffle, step/lunge, other), action speed, focus of visual attention, and time of injury. In addition to descriptive statistics, χ2-tests were used to examine variable associations. A total of 118 video-recorded injuries were obtained. Most sprains were direct contact injuries (n = 72, 61.0%), and the most frequent movement patterns were landing (n = 46), running (n = 15), step/lunge (n = 14), and CoD (n = 13). While direct injuries occurred primarily during landing (43%), non-contact mechanisms (85%) were, by far, the main cause of injury during change of Direction movements (p < 0.01). In the majority of cases, movement speed was moderate (n = 63) and visual attention was directed to the ball (n = 56). Landings are the most frequent cause of ankle sprains in male handball players. Although the largest share, particularly landing-related injuries, results from direct contact, non-contact sprains display a unique pattern as they mostly occur during CoD. Conditioning coaches and health personnel may consider this disparity when designing preventive measures.

title: Age-related slowing of sensorimotor reaction time in masters track and field athletes.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Masters athletes offer a powerful model for understanding how lifelong training shapes age‑related changes in reaction time (RT), a key indicator of sensorimotor performance.
PURPOSE: This cross-sectional study examined RT in masters track and field athletes across age, sex, RT tasks of varying complexity, and event disciplines (endurance, power, sprint).
METHODS: A total of 182 competitors (82 females) from the 2025 World Masters Athletics Championships completed four RT tasks using a wireless light-based testing system.
RESULTS: RT increased progressively with age across all tasks, with the slowest responses consistently observed in athletes ≥80 years old. Female athletes demonstrated slower RT than males, and RT increased systematically with task complexity. Sprint athletes showed faster RT than endurance athletes overall, although event‑specific differences did not persist within age groups. Age was positively associated with RT in all tasks (r = 0.41-0.53), with similar correlation strengths between sexes. Quadratic age effects emerged selectively in male athletes for two-hand simple and step-choice tasks, suggesting accelerated slowing at older ages in tasks requiring greater motor coordination. Linear regression models indicated that RT increased by approximately 3.3-3.6 ms per year of age after adjusting for sex, task, and event discipline, while body composition variables were not significant predictors.
CONCLUSIONS: Although lifelong training is associated with better sensorimotor performance, slower RT remains evident in masters athletes, with consistent sex differences and minimal influence of event discipline.

title: Enhancing Sleep in NCAA Division I Athletes: A Study of Sleep Extension Feasibility.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sleep extension has been shown to improve varied aspects of athletic performance in collegiate athletes. Such studies have been conducted in small cohorts in controlled settings utilizing obsolete monitoring technology. The feasibility of sleep extension has not been evaluated in a broader cohort of collegiate athletes with modern monitoring technology.
HYPOTHESIS: Sleep extension may not be feasible in National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I athletes.
STUDY DESIGN: Crossover study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: Baseline sleep data were collected from NCAA Division I athletes (women's soccer, men's soccer, baseball, and football) during a 2-week period. Subjects were then instructed to extend their total sleep time to 10 hours per night for 2 weeks. All sleep baseline and extension data were collected in the offseason, remote from school examinations. WHOOP bands recorded all sleep metrics. Data were analyzed using paired-samples t tests and Wilcoxon signed rank tests.
RESULTS: A total of 50 subjects (14 female, 36 male) participated. The study compared total sleep time (hours) and sleep consistency (percent) - the stability of sleep-wake schedule over time, between baseline and sleep extension phases. Sample size varied for both metrics, ranging from 46 to 49 participants, respectively. There was a statistically significant increase in sleep consistency during the sleep extension phase (baseline, 60.09 ± 12.6%; extension, 64.42 ± 12.4%; P = 0.02). However, total sleep time showed no significant difference between the 2 phases (baseline, 7.63 ± 0.88 hours; extension, 7.51 ± 0.88 hours; P = 0.27).
CONCLUSION: Extension efforts improved sleep consistency but did not significantly impact total sleep time suggesting that a sleep extension intervention can enhance sleep consistency in NCAA Division I athletes but does not significantly impact total sleep time. Sleep extension may be challenging for collegiate athletes given the time-intensive demands of both academics and sports. While sleep extension may be feasible in professional sports, it does not appear to be so in the college setting.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: While the sleep extension intervention improved sleep consistency, it did not improve total sleep time, questioning the feasibility of sleep extension in collegiate sports.
